jupiter.c: JUPITER: The, Proportion of Jupiter to our Earth, is about 60 to 1. The Periodical Time of Fupiter's Revolution about the Sus, is inthe Space of 12 Years, or 4380 Days and he revolves round his Axis in the Space of 10 Hours; which. very swift Motion may cause that Excess of his Equatorial Diameter above his Polar, which you will find below; whereas in the Sun and Moon, which take, the one. 27, the other 28 Days in their Revolution round their Axis, there is no such Inequality between their Polar and Equatorial Diameters observed. The Mean Distance of Fxpiter from the Sun, according to Kepler 19650; to Bullialdus 522520; according to the Periodical Time of its Revolution y 20116: Such Parts of which the Mean Distance between the Earth and Sun is 100000; that is, about 280862640 Englith Miles. According to Mr. Cafini, Fapiter's greatest Distance from the Earth is 1429 93 his mean Distance 11 s 000; and. leat Distance 87081 Semidiameters of the Earth. And the Diameter of Jupiter is equal to 27 and a Half Semi-diameters of the Earth. Wherefore the Globe of Jupiter must be greater than that of the Earth by 2460 times. The Semi-diameter. of Jupiter, seen from the Sun, is but 19 Seconds,. In the Year 1664, Cazpani ( by the help of an excellent Telescope) observed certain Protuberances and Inequalities in the Surface of this Pla - net. He saw also jin his Body the Shadows of his Satellites, and followed them with his Eye till he saw them go off the. Disk. In the same Year, May the 9 ", 2 Hours P. M. Mr. Hook, with telescope of 12 Foot, observed small Spot in the biggest of the three obscure Belts Of Fapiter; and within two Hours after he found thar the said Spot had moved from Ealt to Weft about half the Length of the Diameter of Jupiter. Mr. Cass ini observed also, near the same Time, a permanent Spot in the Disk of Jupiter; by whose help he not only found that sotiiet turns about upon his own Axis, but also the Time of such Conversion, which he estimates to be 9 Hours, and 56 Minutes.. Which was also confirmed by better Observations of a Spot in the Year 169 t. The Eguatorial Diameter of Jupiter to his Polar one, Sir J /: Newton computes to be as 40 - to 393, Captain Halley, in his Piste to his Catalogue of the Southern Stars, faith, That he found Fupszer to move swifter than he is supposed to do by the Astronomical Tables. The same Learned Person thinks, That the Reason of the Error ( of about 3 or 4 Minutes in Time) of the Tables in calculating the Eclipses of the Sa - Equinoctial Parts, and makes his tellites, arises from some, final Excentricity in the Motion of the Planet, and from the Oval Figure of his Body newly mentioned, whose quick Rotation round his Axis by the ia Coniiape, dilates his meridians much Elliptical, so as to be discernible by the Telescope. he Sun's Heat in Jupiter, is at most not above one twenty fifth part. of what it is with us; and consequently " would be very uncomfortable living there ( if at all possible) for Men of our Constitution; and yet some are very fond of thinking F - peter an excellent Place to live in. The Distance of Jupiter from the Sun, is above five times as great as that of the Earth from the Sun, ( fee Gregory's Affron.) and consequently the Diameter of che Sag to any Eye in Fapiter, will be not a fifth part of what it appears to us, and therefore his Disk will be above 25 times less, and in the same Proportion will bis Light and Heat be. The Artificial Day and Night ( each of Hours) is of the same length in Jupiter all over his Surface; because the Axis of his Diurnal Revolution, is nearly at Right Angles to the Plane of his Annual Orbit round the Sun.. Although Fxpiter hath four Primary Planets below him; yet an Eye placed there, and of no sharper Sight than one of ours, could never behold any One of them, unless as Spots transit ing over the Sun's Disk, when they happen to be between the Jovial Eye and the Sun: For Mars, which goes furthest fall fromthe Sun, will notion Jupiter be seen above 18 Degrees from him; and since that Planet is but final, and reflects but a weak Light, so near the Sun it cannot be visible: So that Saturn is the only Planet that can be seen in Jupiter, except his own four Moons or Satellites. The Sun's Parallax seen from Jupiter, will carce be sensible any more than Saturn's; neither being much above 20 Seconds; so that the Sun's apparent Diameter in 7 xpiter will not be above 6 Minutes: But the outermost of his Satellites will appear almost as great as the Moon doth to us; wz. of five times the Diameter, and 25 times the Disk of the Sun, seen from the same Planet; and if the other Satellites are not less than the outermost, they will yet appear much greater, ( and the Learned Mr. Ange ns conceives them not much less than our Earth) and gives the Planet a good Light in the ie which also can never be there very long. ir. Gregory, ( from whence this comparative Astronomy is colle ed) faith also, that an Astronomer placed in Sups ter, would easily compare the Distances of the four inferior Planets with the Diameters of Jupiter, a 8 we do the Distances of us from the Planets, by comparing thein with the Diameter of the Earth: And this would be done as to the four nearest ones, easier than we compute the Distance of the Moon by the Earth's Diameter; for the Horizontal Parallax of the remotest of the Planets seen from Jupiter, is above twice as pole as the Horizontal Parallax of the Moon seen rom the Earth, and therefore must be very sensible and considerable. And tho the Globe of Fx - peter be vastly large, in comparison of our Earth, yet the Sun's Parallax, when he's beheld from Fapi - ter, will not be quite 20 Seconds, and consequently scarce sensible: Nor will the Parallax of Saturn, ( though when in Opposition to the Sun, and next to Jupiter) be much greater; and therefore " twill be hs esi for the So vial Astronomer to estimate the Distance of Saturn, or of theSun, from that Planet. Ggg 2 Indeed, Indeed, if he can discover that jupiter moves round the Sz, h may be able ( as the Do or shews, Prop. 3.) to determine the Ratio of the Distance of Cantar and Satzrnm from the Sun, otherwise not.:: hates Our Sou ial Astronomer therefore, by the Help of his Senses, Mr hed two kinds of Planets; four nearer to him, which are the Satellites, and two ( as the Suz and Sat wr) more remote; and these latter would appear with a lesser Diameter, the former with a greater: Of the remotest, the Sun would appear in a Diameter about fix Minutes, but the Diameter of Saturn would scarce be of a Minute. 3, Of the four nearer Planets or Satellites, the Fourth would appear to an Eye in xpiter of the Bigness the Moon doth to us; that is, with a Diameter five times greater, and a Disk twenty five times-greater than the Swa doth there: Besides, the four nearer, and apparently greater ones, will be distinguished from the more remote and lesser ones, in this, That in the nearer Planets, che Squares of the Periodick Times, are as the Cubes of their Distances from the Center of Jupiter; which would by no means be true, if any one of the greater were a ta with any one of the lesser. And although the nearer these Planets are, they appear the greater; yet the Sun will be ime nf ely more bright than they; for from their Faces, which depend upon their Situation, with refle to the Sun, they will appear like so many Moons: From whence a Spe tor in jupiter will have four ro of Months, according to the Number of Moons. There will be contained above 2407 of the least Months in a Year, and about half the Number of Months next to these: The Number of the Months of the third Satellite contain'd in a Year, will be nearly subduple of the second, or subquadruple of the first; and the Months of the greatest will be about 254: So that although the Notation of Time be much more intricate in jupiter, by reason of the great Number of Days which their Year contains; yet it is much facilitated by these four kinds of Months; for in the Jeaft Month there are only 4 Days and a Quarter, but in the greatest something more than 40. Betides, these Moons suffer an Eclipse when they, being in Opposition to the Sun, happen to fall into the Shadow of fxpiter; and again, when they, being in Con jun tion with the Sun, prove their Shadows to Jupiter, they make an Eclipse of the Sun to an Eye placed in that Region of Jupiter, where the Shadow falls ( which Region is a very final! part of Fupiter's Surface) just as our Moon does: But because the Orbits of those Moons about Fxpiter, are in a Plane which is inclined to, or makes an Angle with fapister's Orbit about the Sun, and are " all of them nearly in the same Plane, excepting the second, which deviates little; upon this Account, I fay, their Eclipses are Central, and consequently most lasting, when the Sun is in one of the Nodes of those Moons: But when the Sun is out of this Position, the Eclipses may be Total, though not Central, because the Breadth of fupiter's Shadow, is nearly decuple the Breadth of any of the Satellites; and the apparent Diameter of any of those Moons, is nearly quintuple the apparent Diameter of the Sun. And this remarkable Inequality of the Diameters, and the small Inclination the Plane of the Orbits of the Satellites has to the Plane of Fupiter's Orbit round the Sun, is the Reason why in each Revolution there happens Eclipses both of the Satellites and of the Sun, though the Sun be at a consider - ble Distance from the Nodes: And the inferior of these Satellites, though the Sun to a Spe tutor in Jupiter, be ath is greatest Distance from their Nodes, are nevertheless Eclipsed, and Eclipse the Sun; but the remotest of them in this Cafe, for two Years together, escapes falling into Fxpister's Shadow, and Jupiter into its Shadow; and the Phenomena of partial Eclipses in the intermediate Times and Places, will be apparent to a Spe tutor in Jupiter. Farther, it sometimes happens here, that one Moon Eclipses another, whose Phasis is sometimes very different, nay, contrary to the Eclipse of moon, falling into the Shadow of Fxpiter, which was described above; for in this the Oriental Limb is first darkened, and the Occidental Limb emerges Jaft; bur in others of them the Occidental Limb is first darkened, and the Oriental Limb emerges last; and in others contrarily. The Shadow of fapiter, though it go far beyond its Satellites, yet-does not reach ms other Planet, as the Shadow of all other primary Planets do; for no other Planet, except Saturn, could be immerged in it, tho it was infinite; but the Shadow of Jupiter cannot reach Saturn, except the Diameter of Jupiter were half the Diameter of the Sun, and it is scarce of it., If the Surface of Jupiter were chiefly Water, and we suppose the Seas there to be Navigable, the Sailors would have great Advantages, as well be cause the Nights are very short, and very light from the Numbers of their Moons; as because these Moons would be of singular uf to " em in dire ting their Courses, 2 ee For from those manifold Eclipses, the Longitude ofa Place would be easily determined, and Hydrographical Tables accurately construe ted, which is very Advantageous in so salt a Globe as that of Jupiter; whose Surface being Centuple, ( nay, according to Hugens, 400 times as much) the Surface of the Earth would render its Mensuration very laborious: But the Flux and Reflux of the ig occasion'd by these four Moons, ( for the Force of the Sun would be very little there) would be very different, and besides, would be very difficulty brought to a Calculation.

juryincommonlaw.c: JURY, in Common Law, signifies either twenty four or twelve Men sworn to enquire of the Matter of Fa t, and declare the Truth upon such Evidence as shall be delivered them touching the Matter in Question: Of which Fury some may, and some may not be impannel'd: See F. N. B. Fol. 165. In England there are three forts of Trials, oz. one by Parliament, another by Battle, and the third by Assize or Jury. the The By y ra ek ( be bed ee Civil A Criminal), Publick or Private, Personal or " re - : A etre be given them touching the served for the Fa & to a Jury, and as they find it, so passeth the Judgment. This Fury is not only used in Circuits of Justices Ercr ant, but also in other Courts and Matters of Office: And though it appertains to most Courts of the Common Law; yet it is most notoriously in the Half-year Courts of the. Justices Errants, commonly called, the Great Afizes; and in the Quar - ter-Sessions, and in them it is molt ordinarily called a Jury, and that in a Civil Cause; whereas in Other Courts " tis usually called an Jngwe / f, and in the Court-Baron, a Fury of the Homage,; In the General Assize there are usually many Furies, because there be tore of Causes both Civil and Cri - trinal commonly to be tried; whereof one is called, The Grand Jury, andtherelt Petit Furies; whereof it seemeth there should be one in every Hundred. The Grand Fury con fills of Twenty four Grave and Subltantial Gentlemen, or some of the better sort of Yeomen, chosen indifferently by-the Sheriff out of the whole Shire, to confider of all Bills of Indi ment preferred to the Court; which they do either approve, by writing upon them, Billa Vera; or disallow, by indorfing / gworamus. Such as they do approve, if they touch Life and Death, are farther referred to another Jury to be considered of, because the Cafe is of such Importance; but others, Of lighter Moment, are upon their Allowance, without more Work, fined by the Bench; except the Party traverse the Indi & ment, or challenge it for Insufficiency, or remove the Cause to a higher Court by Certiorari; in which two former Cafes it is referred to another Fury; and in the latter, transmitted to a higher: And presently upon the Allowance of this Bill by the Grand In guest, a Man is said to be indi & ed: Such as they disallow are delivered to the Bench, by whom they are forthwith canceled or torn. The Petit Fury consists of Twelve Men at the Tealt, and are impannelled as well upon Criminal, as upon Civil Causes: Those that pass upon Offences of Life and Death, do bring in their Verdi &, either Guilty, or not Guilty; whereupon the Prisoner, if he be found Guilty, is said to be Convicted, and so afterwards receiveth Judgment and Condemnation; or otherwise is acquitted and fer free. Those that pass upon Civil Causes Real, are all, or so many as can conveniently be had, of the same Hundred where the Land or Tenement in Question doth lie, being four at the least; and they, upon due Examination, bring in their Verdi & either for the Demandant or Tenant.
